title: About

About the Author
This project was created by Alexa Titherington as a final data science project at New College of Florida.

Contact: a.titherington30@ncf.edu
GitHub: github.com/alexajt
Project Repository: github.com/alexajt/national-parks



About the Data
All visitation records used in this project come from the official National Park Service Visitor Use Statistics program, accessible through the NPS IRMA Stats Portal and the NPS Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard. The dataset covers calendar-year recreation visits from 2000 through 2025 across 400 reporting units in the National Park System, providing 9,612 verified park-year observations. Annual recreation visits measure entries into park units recorded by NPS field staff, permit systems, and automated counters.

title: Top Parks Over Time
text:
How to read this view
The order changes from year to year, but Great Smoky Mountains, Blue Ridge Parkway, Golden Gate, and other high-volume units often remain among the leaders. Because the plot uses an absolute visit count, a large urban or scenic recreation area can rank above a smaller National Park even though it may offer a very different visitor experience.

title: National Parks, Year by Year: Visitation, 2000–2025
text:
Key Takeaways (2000–2025)

Recreation Areas, Seashores & Parkways lead in typical annual crowd size: Across 1,109 park-year observations (44 units), scenic roadways, seashores, and urban recreation corridors record a median of 1.09 million annual visits.
National Parks & Preserves sustain strong 21st-century attendance: Across 1,953 park-year observations (76 units), flagship National Parks and Preserves hold a median of 520,171 annual visits, with top units exceeding 10 million visits per year.
Historic Sites & National Monuments form the numerical majority of the system: Over two-thirds of all 2000–2025 observations (6,550 of 9,612) belong to historic sites, battlefields, memorials, and monuments, welcoming medians of roughly 97,000 to 113,000 annual visits.

title: Visitation After 2020
text:
Figure 1: Annual recreation visits across the 372 NPS units that reported in every calendar year from 2015 through 2025, summed by designation category and indexed so each category’s 2019 total equals 100.





The chart above tracks combined annual recreation visits for the 372 National Park Service units that reported attendance in every single year from 2015 through 2025, indexed so each category’s 2019 total equals 100.0. In 2020, all four categories declined, but by very different margins: Recreation Areas, Seashores & Parkways (43 units) edged down to 92.9 and National Parks & Preserves (75 units) fell to 75.3, whereas Historic Sites, Battlefields & Memorials (191 units) dropped to 53.8 and National Monuments (63 units) fell to 44.0. By 2021, both National Parks & Preserves (102.9) and Recreation Areas, Seashores & Parkways (101.2) had already exceeded their 2019 totals and remained above that benchmark in 2025 (103.8 and 101.8). In contrast, Historic Sites (86.3 in 2025) and National Monuments (86.2 in 2025) stayed below their 2019 baselines in every post-2020 year.
This split is worth examining because system-wide totals make post-2020 attendance look nearly flat: across these same 372 continuously reporting units, total annual visits moved from 325.0 million in 2019 down to 236.4 million in 2020, back up to 326.7 million in 2024, and to 314.1 million in 2025. Holding the set of reporting units constant shows that the near-return to 2019 aggregate volume is not a uniform recovery across the park system, nor an artifact of newly added park units—higher post-2020 totals at flagship parks and recreation corridors offset persistent shortfalls across more than 250 monuments, battlefields, memorials, and historic sites.
Data source and limitations: Figures come from National Park Service Visitor Use Statistics annual reports compiled in nps_annual_visits_1979_2025.csv. Three limitations apply to this comparison: first, restricting to the 372 continuously reporting units (out of 400 units active at some point during 2015–2025) keeps the panel consistent over time but excludes 28 newer or intermittently reporting units; second, unit categories are grouped from official NPS name suffixes; and third, annual visit counts are purely descriptive—they cannot separate changes in visitor demand from operational factors such as facility closures, construction, timed-entry rules, or counting-method updates, and they provide no information on monthly or seasonal visitation within a year.

title: Rising and Falling Parks
text:
What makes this story useful?
Absolute changes identify the units responsible for the largest shifts in total system attendance. They do not tell us why visitation changed. Temporary closures, construction, reservation systems, counting changes, wildfires, and broader travel patterns could all contribute.
